claim: The conserved eukaryotic/archaeal protein Mbf1 acts with ribosomal proteins Rps3/uS3 and eukaryotic Asc1/RACK1 to prevent frameshifting at inhibitory CGA-CGA codon pairs in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: We show that the conserved eukaryotic/archaeal protein Mbf1 acts with ribosomal proteins Rps3/uS3 and eukaryotic Asc1/RACK1 to prevent frameshifting at inhibitory CGA-CGA codon pairs in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by genetic and molecular data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in RPS3 that allow frameshifting implicate eukaryotic conserved residues near the mRNA entry site.
source: Mutations in RPS3 that allow frameshifting implicate eukaryotic conserved residues near the mRNA entry site.
evidence: Supported by whole genome sequencing data identifying specific RPS3 mutations and structural analysis showing their location near the mRNA entry site.

claim: Mbf1 and Rps3 cooperate to maintain the reading frame of stalled ribosomes.
source: Mbf1 and Rps3 cooperate to maintain the reading frame of stalled ribosomes, while Asc1 also mediates distinct events that result in recruitment of the ribosome quality control complex and mRNA decay.
evidence: Supported by epistasis analysis showing non-additive effects of mutations in MBF1 and RPS3, and by functional assays.

claim: Asc1 mediates distinct events that result in recruitment of the ribosome quality control complex and mRNA decay.
source: Mbf1 and Rps3 cooperate to maintain the reading frame of stalled ribosomes, while Asc1 also mediates distinct events that result in recruitment of the ribosome quality control complex and mRNA decay.
evidence: Supported by data showing increased mRNA levels in asc1Δ mutants and by citations to previous work on Asc1's role in RQC.

claim: Frameshifting occurs through a +1 shift with a CGA codon in the P site.
source: Frameshifting occurs through a +1 shift with a CGA codon in the P site and involves competition between codons entering the A site, implying that the wobble interaction of the P site codon destabilizes translation elongation.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry analysis of purified frameshifted peptides identifying the specific frameshift mechanism.

claim: Frameshifting involves competition between codons entering the A site.
source: Frameshifting occurs through a +1 shift with a CGA codon in the P site and involves competition between codons entering the A site, implying that the wobble interaction of the P site codon destabilizes translation elongation.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing that overexpression of tRNAs corresponding to in-frame or +1 frame codons modulates frameshifting efficiency.

claim: The wobble interaction of the P site codon destabilizes translation elongation.
source: Frameshifting occurs through a +1 shift with a CGA codon in the P site and involves competition between codons entering the A site, implying that the wobble interaction of the P site codon destabilizes translation elongation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CGA codons (decoded by wobble interaction) in the P site are associated with frameshifting.

claim: Eukaryotes have evolved unique mechanisms involving both a universally conserved ribosome component and two eukaryotic-specific proteins to maintain the reading frame at ribosome stalls.
source: Thus, eukaryotes have evolved unique mechanisms involving both a universally conserved ribosome component and two eukaryotic-specific proteins to maintain the reading frame at ribosome stalls.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing that Rps3 (universally conserved), Mbf1 (eukaryotic/archaeal), and Asc1 (eukaryotic) work together to prevent frameshifting.

claim: Reading frame maintenance is challenging because multiple movements of the tRNAs and mRNA as well as conformational changes within the ribosome itself are required to complete a single elongation cycle.
source: Reading frame maintenance is challenging because multiple movements of the tRNAs and mRNA as well as conformational changes within the ribosome itself are required to complete a single elongation cycle (Noller et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on ribosome dynamics during translation.

claim: The tRNA acceptor stems move within the large subunit during formation of the hybrid state.
source: For instance, the tRNA acceptor stems move within the large subunit during formation of the hybrid state, while the joining of EF-G-GTP (eEF2 in eukaryotes) results in additional movement of tRNA, and finally completion of translocation, driven by Pi release, requires additional movements (Belardinelli et al., 2016; Brilot et al., 2013; Noller et al., 2017; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Ramrath et al., 2013; Ratje et al., 2010; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies of translation.

claim: The joining of EF-G-GTP (eEF2 in eukaryotes) results in additional movement of tRNA.
source: For instance, the tRNA acceptor stems move within the large subunit during formation of the hybrid state, while the joining of EF-G-GTP (eEF2 in eukaryotes) results in additional movement of tRNA, and finally completion of translocation, driven by Pi release, requires additional movements (Belardinelli et al., 2016; Brilot et al., 2013; Noller et al., 2017; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Ramrath et al., 2013; Ratje et al., 2010; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies of translation.

claim: Completion of translocation, driven by Pi release, requires additional movements.
source: For instance, the tRNA acceptor stems move within the large subunit during formation of the hybrid state, while the joining of EF-G-GTP (eEF2 in eukaryotes) results in additional movement of tRNA, and finally completion of translocation, driven by Pi release, requires additional movements (Belardinelli et al., 2016; Brilot et al., 2013; Noller et al., 2017; Pulk and Cate, 2013; Ramrath et al., 2013; Ratje et al., 2010; Tourigny et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to structural and biochemical studies of translation.

claim: The relative position of the tRNA anticodon to the mRNA codon must be maintained throughout all of the events of the elongation cycle.
source: To accomplish this cycle, many interactions between the tRNAs and ribosome are disrupted, and new interactions are created, but the relative position of the tRNA anticodon to the mRNA codon must be maintained throughout all of these events (Noller et al., 2017; Dever et al., 2018; Rodnina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on translation mechanisms.

claim: Mechanisms exist to prevent slippage during transitions in the elongation cycle.
source: Thus, it is critical that mechanisms exist to prevent slippage during these transitions.
evidence: This is inferred from the complexity of the elongation cycle and the need to maintain reading frame.

claim: A swivel of the 30S head relative to the 30S body to form a contracted mRNA tunnel downstream of the A site prior to translocation contributes to reading frame maintenance.
source: Structural features that contribute to reading frame maintenance, inferred from analysis of prokaryotic translation intermediates, include a swivel of the 30S head relative to the 30S body to form a contracted mRNA tunnel downstream of the A site prior to translocation (Jenner et al., 2010; Schuwirth et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of bacterial ribosomes.

claim: During translocation, two conserved bases in the 16S rRNA intercalate into different positions of the mRNA to prevent slippage.
source: In addition, during translocation, two conserved bases in the 16S rRNA intercalate into different positions of the mRNA to prevent slippage (Zhou et al., 2013), while domain IV of EF-G contacts the codon and tRNA in the A/P site and h44 of 16S rRNA, likely coupling mRNA and tRNA movement (Ramrath et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of bacterial ribosomes during translocation.

claim: Domain IV of EF-G contacts the codon and tRNA in the A/P site and h44 of 16S rRNA, likely coupling mRNA and tRNA movement.
source: In addition, during translocation, two conserved bases in the 16S rRNA intercalate into different positions of the mRNA to prevent slippage (Zhou et al., 2013), while domain IV of EF-G contacts the codon and tRNA in the A/P site and h44 of 16S rRNA, likely coupling mRNA and tRNA movement (Ramrath et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies of bacterial ribosomes during translocation.

claim: Mutants that affect several tRNA modifications in both bacteria and eukaryotes result in increased frameshifting.
source: Mutants that affect several such modifications in both bacteria and eukaryotes result in increased frameshifting (Atkins and Björk, 2009; Jäger et al., 2013; Tükenmez et al., 2015; Urbonavicius et al., 2001; Waas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic studies of tRNA modifications.

claim: A cross-strand base stacking interaction between a modified ms2i6A37 in an E. coli tRNAPhe and the mRNA codon is proposed to prevent slippage of P site tRNA on the mRNA.
source: Moreover, a cross-strand base stacking interaction between a modified ms2i6A37 in an E. coli tRNAPhe and the mRNA codon is proposed to prevent slippage of P site tRNA on the mRNA (Jenner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study of bacterial ribosomes.

claim: Ribosomes do move into alternative reading frames in response to specific sequences and structures in mRNA.
source: Nevertheless, ribosomes do move into alternative reading frames in response to specific sequences and structures in mRNA (Atkins and Björk, 2009; Dever et al., 2018; Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on programmed frameshifting.

claim: Ribosomal plasticity with respect to reading frame movement is an integral function of the translation machinery.
source: The existence of such events has implied that ribosomal plasticity with respect to reading frame movement is an integral function of the translation machinery.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that programmed frameshifting occurs in many organisms.

claim: The common feature of all frameshifting events in bacteria to humans is that the ribosome stalls.
source: The common feature of all frameshifting events in bacteria to humans is that the ribosome stalls (Dever et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on translation mechanisms.

claim: The stall can be mediated by combined effects of the A and P site codons.
source: The stall can be mediated by combined effects of the A and P site codons (Farabaugh et al., 2006; Gamble et al., 2016), by the presence of downstream structures, or by an upstream Shine-Dalgarno sequence in bacteria (Caliskan et al., 2014; Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on frameshifting mechanisms.

claim: The stall can be mediated by the presence of downstream structures.
source: The stall can be mediated by combined effects of the A and P site codons (Farabaugh et al., 2006; Gamble et al., 2016), by the presence of downstream structures, or by an upstream Shine-Dalgarno sequence in bacteria (Caliskan et al., 2014; Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on frameshifting mechanisms.

claim: The stall can be mediated by an upstream Shine-Dalgarno sequence in bacteria.
source: The stall can be mediated by combined effects of the A and P site codons (Farabaugh et al., 2006; Gamble et al., 2016), by the presence of downstream structures, or by an upstream Shine-Dalgarno sequence in bacteria (Caliskan et al., 2014; Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on frameshifting mechanisms in bacteria.

claim: Additional sequences or protein factors are frequently required to mediate efficient frameshifting.
source: Analysis of programmed frameshifting indicates that additional sequences or protein factors are frequently required to mediate efficient frameshifting (Atkins and Björk, 2009; Dinman, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews on programmed frameshifting.

claim: +1 programmed frameshifting events are frequently enhanced by stimulatory sequences.
source: For instance, +1 programmed frameshifting events are frequently enhanced by stimulatory sequences, although the role of these sequences is not always clear (Guarraia et al., 2007; Taliaferro and Farabaugh, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on +1 frameshifting.

claim: In bacteria, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by deletions within the C terminal domain of ribosomal protein uS9, which contacts the P site tRNA anticodon loop.
source: In bacteria, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by deletions within the C terminal domain of ribosomal protein uS9, which contacts the P site tRNA anticodon loop (Jäger et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on bacterial ribosomal proteins.

claim: In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, programmed frameshifting in the L-A virus is affected by mutations in 5S rRNA or its interactors uL18 or uL5, that also contact the P site tRNA.
source: In the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, programmed frameshifting in the L-A virus is affected by mutations in 5S rRNA or its interactors uL18 or uL5, that also contact the P site tRNA (Meskauskas and Dinman, 2001; Rhodin and Dinman, 2010; Smith et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on yeast ribosomal components.

claim: Frameshifting mutations are suppressed by a mutation in the yeast RPS3, although this mutation does not affect a tRNA contact.
source: Frameshifting mutations are also suppressed by a mutation in the yeast RPS3, although this mutation does not affect a tRNA contact (Hendrick et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on yeast RPS3.

claim: Frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in both EF-1α, which delivers tRNA to the ribosome, and in SUP35, encoding the translation termination factor eRF3.
source: For instance, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in both EF-1α, which delivers tRNA to the ribosome (Sandbaken and Culbertson, 1988), and in SUP35, encoding the translation termination factor eRF3 (Wilson and Culbertson, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on translation factors.

claim: miRNAs can affect the efficiency of programmed frameshifting, for instance at CCR5 in humans.
source: Third, miRNAs can affect the efficiency of programmed frameshifting, for instance at CCR5 in humans (Belew et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on miRNA effects on frameshifting.

claim: In yeast, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in MBF1, encoding Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1.
source: For instance, in yeast, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in MBF1, encoding Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1 (Hendrick et al., 2001), or in EBS1 (Ford et al., 2006), while in the porcine virus PRRSV, the RNA binding protein nsp1β stimulates both −1 and −2 frameshifting events (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on yeast MBF1.

claim: In yeast, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in EBS1.
source: For instance, in yeast, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in MBF1, encoding Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1 (Hendrick et al., 2001), or in EBS1 (Ford et al., 2006), while in the porcine virus PRRSV, the RNA binding protein nsp1β stimulates both −1 and −2 frameshifting events (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on yeast EBS1.

claim: In the porcine virus PRRSV, the RNA binding protein nsp1β stimulates both −1 and −2 frameshifting events.
source: For instance, in yeast, frameshifting mutations are suppressed by mutations in MBF1, encoding Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1 (Hendrick et al., 2001), or in EBS1 (Ford et al., 2006), while in the porcine virus PRRSV, the RNA binding protein nsp1β stimulates both −1 and −2 frameshifting events (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on PRRSV frameshifting.

claim: In bacteria, ribosome stalls due to limited availability or functionality of tRNA seem to suffice to cause frameshifting.
source: In bacteria, ribosome stalls due to limited availability or functionality of tRNA seem to suffice to cause frameshifting (Gurvich et al., 2005; Seidman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on bacterial frameshifting.

claim: In wild type yeast, ribosomes stall at CGA codon repeats, which inhibit translation due to wobble decoding of CGA by its native tRNAArg(ICG).
source: In wild type yeast, ribosomes stall at CGA codon repeats, which inhibit translation due to wobble decoding of CGA by its native tRNAArg(ICG) (Letzring et al., 2010; Letzring et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on CGA codon effects in yeast.

claim: Frameshifting was not detected at CGA codon repeats in wild type yeast.
source: Although frameshifting was detected at several underrepresented heptanucleotide sequences in yeast (Shah et al., 2002), it was not detected at CGA codon repeats (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on frameshifting in yeast.

claim: Eukaryotes have evolved new pathways to regulate inefficient translation events, such as the Ribosome Quality Control (RQC) pathway.
source: Instead, eukaryotes have evolved new pathways to regulate inefficient translation events, such as the Ribosome Quality Control (RQC) pathway, in which these stalled ribosomes undergo ubiquitination of ribosomal proteins, followed by dissociation of the subunits, and recruitment of the RQC Complex, which mediates CAT tailing and degradation of the nascent polypeptide (Bengtson and Joazeiro, 2010; Brandman and Hegde, 2016; Brandman et al., 2012; Defenouillère et al., 2013; Joazeiro, 2017; Kostova et al., 2017; Shao et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2015; Verma et al., 2013; Wilson et al., 2007; Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Simms et al., 2017b; Sitron et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on the RQC pathway.

claim: The ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 mediates RQC events.
source: The ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 mediates these events (Brandman et al., 2012; Kuroha et al., 2010); in the absence of Asc1, ribosomes fail to engage the RQC (Sitron et al., 2017), and also undergo substantial frameshifting at CGA codon repeats (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Asc1 function.

claim: In the absence of Asc1, ribosomes fail to engage the RQC.
source: The ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 mediates these events (Brandman et al., 2012; Kuroha et al., 2010); in the absence of Asc1, ribosomes fail to engage the RQC (Sitron et al., 2017), and also undergo substantial frameshifting at CGA codon repeats (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Asc1 function.

claim: In the absence of Asc1, ribosomes undergo substantial frameshifting at CGA codon repeats.
source: The ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1 mediates these events (Brandman et al., 2012; Kuroha et al., 2010); in the absence of Asc1, ribosomes fail to engage the RQC (Sitron et al., 2017), and also undergo substantial frameshifting at CGA codon repeats (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on Asc1 and frameshifting.

claim: Asc1 sits on the outside of the ribosome at the mRNA exit tunnel and likely functions as scaffold for recruitment of other proteins, such as the E3 ubiquitin ligase Hel2/mammalian ZNF598 and Slh1.
source: However, Asc1 sits on the outside of the ribosome at the mRNA exit tunnel and likely functions as scaffold for recruitment of other proteins, such as the E3 ubiquitin ligase Hel2/mammalian ZNF598 and Slh1 (Juszkiewicz and Hegde, 2017; Matsuo et al., 2017; Simms et al., 2017b; Sitron et al., 2017; Sundaramoorthy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and functional studies on Asc1.

claim: Introduction of the non-native tRNAArg(UCG)* suppressed the Ura+ phenotype of mutant P25 at 30°C.
source: Expression of the non-native tRNAArg(UCG)* suppressed the Ura+ phenotype of mutant P25 at 30°C.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and described in the text, demonstrating that efficient decoding of CGA codons suppresses frameshifting.

claim: Expression of the exact match tRNAArg(UCG)* results in efficient decoding of CGA codons and suppresses their inhibitory effects on gene expression.
source: We have shown previously that expression of this exact match tRNAArg(UCG)* results in efficient decoding of CGA codons and suppresses their inhibitory effects on gene expression (Letzring et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The Ura+, GFP+ phenotype of mutant P25 was due to frameshifting that occurs when the ribosome translates CGA codon repeats inefficiently.
source: Thus, the Ura+, GFP+ phenotype of this mutant was due to frameshifting that occurs when the ribosome translates CGA codon repeats inefficiently.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of the phenotype by the exact match tRNA.

claim: Mutations in the yeast gene MBF1, Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1, were responsible for the defects in reading frame maintenance in recessive high GFP mutants.
source: We demonstrated that mutations in the yeast gene MBF1, Multi-protein Bridging Factor 1, were responsible for the defects in reading frame maintenance in recessive high GFP mutants.
evidence: This is supported by complementation analysis and sequencing of mutants.

claim: A plasmid with only the MBF1 gene complemented the frameshifting Ura+ phenotype of two mutants.
source: First, a plasmid with only the MBF1 gene complemented the frameshifting Ura+ phenotype of two mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Deletion of MBF1 in the parent selection strain converted that strain from GFP- to GFP+, similar to deletion of ASC1.
source: Second, deletion of MBF1 in the parent selection strain (Figure 1A) converted that strain from GFP- to GFP+, similar to deletion of ASC1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 19/19 mutants tested contain mutations in the MBF1 gene.
source: Third, 19/19 mutants tested contain mutations in the MBF1 gene.
evidence: This is based on sequencing of the MBF1 gene in mutants.

claim: Point mutations isolated in the selection are located at conserved residues near the junctions between two domains.
source: Point mutations isolated in our selection are located at conserved residues near the junctions between two domains (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with alignment of Mbf1 sequences.

claim: MBF1 is a highly conserved gene in eukaryotes and archaea, generally less than 160 amino acids with an N-terminal Mbf1-specific domain (that differs between archaea and eukaryotes) and a conserved cro-like helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain.
source: MBF1 is a highly conserved gene in eukaryotes and archaea, generally less than 160 amino acids with an N-terminal Mbf1-specific domain (that differs between archaea and eukaryotes) and a conserved cro-like helix-turn-helix (HTH) domain (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Mbf1 was initially identified as a transcription co-activator in Bombyx mori.
source: Mbf1, which was initially identified as a transcription co-activator in Bombyx mori (Li et al., 1994; Takemaru et al., 1997), has been implicated in a similar function in yeast, in this case, interacting with the Gcn4, transcription regulator of the general amino acid control pathway (Takemaru et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Mbf1 function.

claim: Mbf1 has been implicated in a similar function in yeast, interacting with the Gcn4, transcription regulator of the general amino acid control pathway.
source: Mbf1, which was initially identified as a transcription co-activator in Bombyx mori (Li et al., 1994; Takemaru et al., 1997), has been implicated in a similar function in yeast, in this case, interacting with the Gcn4, transcription regulator of the general amino acid control pathway (Takemaru et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on yeast Mbf1.

claim: Two frameshifting point mutants (mbf1-K64E and mbf1-I85T) exhibit no growth defect even on high concentrations of 3-AT.
source: In testing sensitivity to 3-aminotriazole (3-AT) (Hilton et al., 1965; Schürch et al., 1974), a phenotype of gcn4 mutants due to inability to induce expression of HIS3, we found that two frameshifting point mutants (mbf1-K64E and mbf1-I85T) exhibit no growth defect even on high concentrations of 3-AT (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Deletion of GCN4 does not affect frameshifting at CGA codon repeats in an asc1Δ mutant.
source: Moreover, deletion of GCN4 does not affect frameshifting at CGA codon repeats in an asc1Δ mutant (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It is unlikely that the defect in reading frame maintenance in mbf1 mutants is related to GCN4.
source: Thus, it is unlikely that the defect in reading frame maintenance in our mbf1 mutants is related to GCN4.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of 3-AT sensitivity and the lack of effect of GCN4 deletion on frameshifting.

claim: Mbf1 has been implicated in translation, based on isolation of mutations in yeast MBF1 that suppress frameshifting mutations.
source: However, Mbf1 has also been implicated in translation, based on isolation of mutations in yeast MBF1 that suppress frameshifting mutations (Hendrick et al., 2001), and the weak association of the archaeal homolog with ribosomes (Blombach et al., 2014), but there is no information on its molecular role in translation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The archaeal homolog of Mbf1 weakly associates with ribosomes.
source: However, Mbf1 has also been implicated in translation, based on isolation of mutations in yeast MBF1 that suppress frameshifting mutations (Hendrick et al., 2001), and the weak association of the archaeal homolog with ribosomes (Blombach et al., 2014), but there is no information on its molecular role in translation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on archaeal Mbf1.

claim: Each dominant mutant contains a single amino acid change (S104Y and G121D) in RPS3.
source: To identify the mutated gene(s) in our dominant mutants, we performed whole genome sequencing in two MATα mutants and found that each mutant contains a single amino acid change (S104Y and G121D) in RPS3.
evidence: This is based on whole genome sequencing data.

claim: The two dominant MATa mutants also contain mutations in the RPS3 gene (L113F and a duplication of N22 to A30).
source: Similarly, the two dominant MATa mutants also contain mutations in the RPS3 gene (L113F and a duplication of N22 to A30).
evidence: This is based on sequencing of the RPS3 gene.

claim: RPS3 encodes a universally conserved ribosomal protein, a core component of the mRNA entry tunnel with a eukaryotic-specific C-terminal extension that interacts with Asc1.
source: RPS3 encodes a universally conserved ribosomal protein, a core component of the mRNA entry tunnel with a eukaryotic-specific C-terminal extension that interacts with Asc1 (Rabl et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study.

claim: One known mutation in RPS3 (K108E) affects reading frame maintenance.
source: One known mutation in RPS3 (K108E) affects reading frame maintenance (Hendrick et al., 2001), while others affect different aspects of translation, from initiation to quality control (Dong et al., 2017; Graifer et al., 2014; Limoncelli et al., 2017; Takyar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The three residues S104, L113 and G121 implicated in reading frame maintenance, as well as K108, are all found in two α-helices near the mRNA entry tunnel of the ribosome.
source: The three residues S104, L113 and G121 implicated in reading frame maintenance in our study, as well as K108, are all found in two α-helices near the mRNA entry tunnel of the ribosome; these residues reside on the surface of the ribosome and could interact with mRNA or proteins outside of the ribosome (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with structural analysis.

claim: These residues (S104, L113, G121, K108) reside on the surface of the ribosome and could interact with mRNA or proteins outside of the ribosome.
source: The three residues S104, L113 and G121 implicated in reading frame maintenance in our study, as well as K108, are all found in two α-helices near the mRNA entry tunnel of the ribosome; these residues reside on the surface of the ribosome and could interact with mRNA or proteins outside of the ribosome (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The identity of all four of these residues (S104, L113, G121, K108) is conserved in eukaryotes, but different in bacteria and archaea.
source: Moreover, the identity of all four of these residues is conserved in eukaryotes, but different in bacteria and archaea (Graifer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on ribosomal protein conservation.

claim: The RPS3-K108E mutation allows frameshifting but does not affect in-frame expression.
source: We initially examined the effect of the RPS3-K108E mutation on both frameshifting and in-frame expression downstream of CGA codon repeats, and found that this mutation allows frameshifting but does not affect in-frame expression.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The RPS3-K108E mutation has only minor effects on the polysome to monosome ratio.
source: We chose the K108E mutation because it is known to have only minor effects on the polysome to monosome ratio (Dong et al., 2017), consistent with few nonspecific effects on translation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Neither the RPS3 mutant nor a mbf1Δ mutant had a substantial effect on GFP/RFP fluorescence (protein), mRNA or protein/mRNA of reporters with CGA or AGA codon repeats in-frame.
source: Neither the RPS3 mutant nor a mbf1Δ mutant had a substantial effect on GFP/RFP fluorescence (protein), mRNA or protein/mRNA of reporters with CGA or AGA codon repeats in-frame (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The RPS3-K108E and mbf1Δ mutants each caused substantially increased frameshifted GFP/RFP protein and protein/mRNA in the construct with four CGA codons, but had only small effects on GFP/RFP mRNA.
source: The RPS3-K108E and mbf1Δ mutants each caused substantially increased frameshifted GFP/RFP protein and protein/mRNA in the construct with four CGA codons, but had only small effects on GFP/RFP mRNA; no frameshifting was seen with four AGA codons (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: No frameshifting was seen with four AGA codons in RPS3-K108E and mbf1Δ mutants.
source: The RPS3-K108E and mbf1Δ mutants each caused substantially increased frameshifted GFP/RFP protein and protein/mRNA in the construct with four CGA codons, but had only small effects on GFP/RFP mRNA; no frameshifting was seen with four AGA codons (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The double mutant RPS3-K108E mbf1Δ exhibited only a slight increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein relative to either single mutant.
source: Instead, we found that the double mutant RPS3-K108E mbf1Δ exhibited only a slight increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein; this increase is likely due to a slight increase in GFP/RFP mRNA relative to either single mutant, resulting in nearly identical protein/mRNA from the mbf1Δ and RPS3-K108E mbf1Δ mutants (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Each single mutant (RPS3-S104Y and G121D) exhibited frameshifting and the double mutants exhibited similar amounts of frameshifted GFP/RFP to that in the mbf1Δ strain.
source: In these cases again, each single mutant exhibited frameshifting and the double mutants exhibited similar amounts of frameshifted GFP/RFP to that in the mbf1Δ strain, although even an additive effect would be easily detectable (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Mbf1 and the two α-helices in the N-terminal Rps3 protein have related roles in reading frame maintenance.
source: Thus, we think it is likely that Mbf1 and the two α-helices in the N-terminal Rps3 protein have related roles in reading frame maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis showing non-additive effects.

claim: Introduction of additional copies of the MBF1 gene into RPS3-S104Y or G121D mutants resulted in reduced expression of frameshifted GFP.
source: We found that introduction of additional copies of the MBF1 gene into either of these mutants resulted in reduced expression of frameshifted GFP (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Frameshifted GFP was reduced to 30% in the S104Y mutant and to 60% in the G121D mutant when MBF1 was overexpressed.
source: Frameshifted GFP was reduced to 30% in the S104Y mutant and to 60% in the G121D mutant (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Growth on media lacking uracil was severely compromised in the RPS3-S104Y mutant when MBF1 was expressed on a multi-copy plasmid, relative to an empty vector control.
source: Similarly, growth on media lacking uracil was severely compromised in the RPS3-S104Y mutant when MBF1 was expressed on a multi-copy plasmid, relative to an empty vector control (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), although both strains grow equally well on SD-Leu media.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: These RPS3 mutations reduce Mbf1 function.
source: These observations are consistent with the idea that Mbf1 and Rps3 play similar roles in reading frame maintenance and support the idea that these RPS3 mutations reduce Mbf1 function.
evidence: This is inferred from the suppression of frameshifting by MBF1 overexpression in RPS3 mutants.

claim: Asc1 is required for reading frame maintenance at CGA codon repeats.
source: Since Asc1 is also required for reading frame maintenance at CGA codon repeats (Wolf and Grayhack, 2015), we examined the relationship between MBF1 and ASC1 on both frameshifting and in-frame expression, comparing GFP/RFP in the single mutants to that in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutant.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Asc1 affects expression (both in-frame and +1 frame) downstream of four CGA codons.
source: Asc1 is known to affect expression (both in-frame and +1 frame) downstream of four CGA codons (Letzring et al., 2013; Wolf and Grayhack, 2015), but we previously noted that inhibitory effects of CGA codons are mediated by CGA codon pairs (Gamble et al., 2016; Letzring et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibitory effects of CGA codons are mediated by CGA codon pairs.
source: Asc1 is known to affect expression (both in-frame and +1 frame) downstream of four CGA codons (Letzring et al., 2013; Wolf and Grayhack, 2015), but we previously noted that inhibitory effects of CGA codons are mediated by CGA codon pairs (Gamble et al., 2016; Letzring et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of ASC1 resulted in increased protein and mRNA levels of reporters with in-frame CGA-CGA codon pairs.
source: As expected based on a previous report (Sitron et al., 2017), deletion of ASC1 resulted in increased protein and mRNA levels of reporters with in-frame CGA-CGA codon pairs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of MBF1 did not affect protein or mRNA levels substantially.
source: By contrast, deletion of MBF1 did not affect protein or mRNA levels substantially (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and supplementary figures.

claim: Asc1 has a unique role in regulating mRNA and RQC recruitment at CGA codon pairs.
source: Thus, Asc1 clearly has a unique role in regulating mRNA and RQC recruitment at CGA codon pairs, but overall expression, measured as protein/mRNA, of all in-frame reporters is similar in the wild type, asc1Δ, mbf1Δ, and asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased mRNA but similar protein/mRNA in asc1Δ mutants.

claim: Overall expression, measured as protein/mRNA, of all in-frame reporters is similar in the wild type, asc1Δ, mbf1Δ, and asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutants.
source: Thus, Asc1 clearly has a unique role in regulating mRNA and RQC recruitment at CGA codon pairs, but overall expression, measured as protein/mRNA, of all in-frame reporters is similar in the wild type, asc1Δ, mbf1Δ, and asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutants (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The increase in mRNA in an asc1Δ mutant does not explain the increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein in this mutant.
source: However, the increase in mRNA in an asc1Δ mutant does not explain the increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein in this mutant. That is, the 2.7-fold increase in GFP/RFP mRNA from the +1 reporter in an asc1Δ mutant (relative to the wild type) cannot account for the >50 fold increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP fluorescence (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A by comparing the fold-change in mRNA versus protein.

claim: An asc1Δ mutant exhibits a defect in reading frame maintenance.
source: Thus, an asc1Δ mutant clearly exhibits a defect in reading frame maintenance.
evidence: This is inferred from the disproportionate increase in frameshifted protein relative to mRNA increase.

claim: The level of frameshifted GFP/RFP protein per mRNA was very similar in the single mbf1Δ mutant to that in the double asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant.
source: In fact, the level of frameshifted GFP/RFP protein per mRNA was very similar in the single mbf1Δ mutant to that in the double asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: These results are most consistent with a single pathway of reading frame maintenance, which Asc1 influences.
source: These results are most consistent with a single pathway of reading frame maintenance, which Asc1 influences.
evidence: This is inferred from the epistasis analysis showing similar protein/mRNA in mbf1Δ and asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutants.

claim: The amount of full-length GFP protein in the Western blot corresponds to the GFP/RFP values obtained from flow analysis.
source: The amount of full-length GFP protein in the Western blot corresponds to the GFP/RFP values obtained from flow analysis (Figure 3B) indicating that +1 GFP/RFP signal in our mutants is due to frameshifting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by Western blot analysis.

claim: Expression of MBF1 on a multi-copy plasmid suppressed frameshifting in the asc1Δ strain to 1/3 that seen with an empty vector, but did not affect in-frame expression.
source: We found that expression of MBF1 on a multi-copy plasmid did suppress frameshifting in the asc1Δ strain to 1/3 that seen with an empty vector, but did not affect in-frame expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The overproduction of Mbf1 was not complementing a reduced abundance of Mbf1 in the asc1Δ mutant.
source: The overproduction of Mbf1 was not complementing a reduced abundance of Mbf1 in this mutant. We did not detect a reduction in Mbf1-HA (which complements the mbf1Δ mutant) in the asc1Δ strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), although asc1 mutants generally exhibit a defect in expression of small proteins (Thompson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A by Western blot analysis.

claim: Additional copies of ASC1 did not suppress frameshifting in an mbf1Δ mutant.
source: We also considered that mbf1 mutants might require additional Asc1 protein, but additional copies of ASC1 did not suppress frameshifting in an mbf1Δ mutant (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The frameshifted GFP/RFP fluorescence in the asc1Δ strain is likely a result of both an increase in mRNA and a defect in the Mbf1 pathway.
source: Thus, the frameshifted GFP/RFP fluorescence in the asc1Δ strain is likely a result of both an increase in mRNA and a defect in the Mbf1 pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that MBF1 overexpression suppresses frameshifting in asc1Δ mutants.

claim: Mbf1 and Asc1 contribute in distinct ways to the response to CGA codon pairs.
source: We infer that Mbf1 and Asc1 contribute in distinct ways to the response to CGA codon pairs, but we do not know if Asc1 also has a direct role in the reading frame maintenance pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing different effects of asc1Δ and mbf1Δ on mRNA levels and frameshifting.

claim: Mbf1 and Asc1 act on the same inhibitory codon pairs.
source: We found that Mbf1 and Asc1 act on the same inhibitory codon pairs.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that frameshifting occurs at the same codon pairs in both mutants.

claim: Frameshifting occurs with high efficiency at three codon pairs (CGA-CGA, CGA-CGG, and CGA-CCG) in the mbf1Δ mutant.
source: Frameshifting occurs with high efficiency at three codon pairs (CGA-CGA, CGA-CGG, and CGA-CCG) in the mbf1Δ mutant (Figure 4A), the only three pairs at which Asc1 substantially modulates in–frame expression levels relative to synonymous optimal reporters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CGA-CGA, CGA-CGG, and CGA-CCG are the only three pairs at which Asc1 substantially modulates in-frame expression levels relative to synonymous optimal reporters.
source: Frameshifting occurs with high efficiency at three codon pairs (CGA-CGA, CGA-CGG, and CGA-CCG) in the mbf1Δ mutant (Figure 4A), the only three pairs at which Asc1 substantially modulates in–frame expression levels relative to synonymous optimal reporters (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Frameshifted GFP/RFP for CGA-CCG and CGA-CGA is greater in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant than in the mbf1Δ single mutant.
source: As might be expected, frameshifted GFP/RFP for CGA-CCG and CGA-CGA is greater in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant than in the mbf1Δ single mutant (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Frameshifting at CGA-CGG is remarkably high (~76%).
source: Surprisingly, this is not true for the CGA-CGG construct at which frameshifting is remarkably high (~76% based on data from Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is calculated from data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Lower levels of frameshifting were detected at 4 additional pairs (CGA-AUA, CGA-CUG, CGA-GCG, and CUC-CCG) in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant, but not in the mbf1Δ single mutant.
source: Lower levels of frameshifting were also detected at 4 additional pairs (CGA-AUA, CGA-CUG, CGA-GCG, and CUC-CCG) in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant, but not in the mbf1Δ single mutant (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Frameshifting was detected at the seven most slowly translated codon pairs in the yeast genome.
source: Analysis of these seven codon pairs indicates that frameshifting was detected at the seven most slowly translated codon pairs in the yeast genome [based on analysis in (Gamble et al., 2016)] and at every inhibitory pair with CGA in the 5' position, consistent with slow decoding of CGA in the P site (Tunney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous studies on codon translation rates.

claim: Frameshifting was detected at every inhibitory pair with CGA in the 5' position, consistent with slow decoding of CGA in the P site.
source: Analysis of these seven codon pairs indicates that frameshifting was detected at the seven most slowly translated codon pairs in the yeast genome [based on analysis in (Gamble et al., 2016)] and at every inhibitory pair with CGA in the 5' position, consistent with slow decoding of CGA in the P site (Tunney et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on codon decoding rates.

claim: Frameshifted GFP/RFP protein from both +1 and −1 constructs was detectable in wild type at a no-go sequence, greater in each single mutant and even greater in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant.
source: In accordance with this idea, frameshifted GFP/RFP protein from both +1 and −1 constructs was detectable in wild type, greater in each single mutant and even greater in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mbf1 and Asc1 mutants did not affect frameshifting efficiency at the programmed frameshift site for TY1.
source: By contrast, these mutants did not affect frameshifting efficiency at the programmed frameshift site for TY1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) (Belcourt and Farabaugh, 1990).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Mbf1 and Asc1 regulate reading frame maintenance at a translational pause (no-go site), but do not enhance frameshifting at site in which translational slippage is encoded.
source: Thus, Mbf1 and Asc1 regulate reading frame maintenance at a translational pause (no-go site), but do not enhance frameshifting at site in which translational slippage is encoded.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing frameshifting at no-go sites but not at TY1 programmed frameshift sites.

claim: The first CGA-CGG codon pair was responsible for highly efficient frameshifting.
source: To define the source of efficient frameshifting in the CGA-CGG reporter, which has 3 CGA-CGG pairs (Figure 4A), we initially determined that the first CGA-CGG codon pair was responsible for highly efficient frameshifting (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Either of two changes to the sequence downstream of the CGA-CGG pair (one a point mutation and another a codon insertion) eliminated efficient frameshifting in all three mutant strains.
source: To define the sequence requirements for efficient frameshifting, we varied the sequences surrounding this single CGA-CGG pair and measured frameshifted GFP/RFP in the various mutants. Either of two changes to the sequence downstream of the CGA-CGG pair (one a point mutation and another a codon insertion) eliminated efficient frameshifting in all three mutant strains (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Altering the two nucleotides downstream of the first codon pair in the three codon pair reporter reduced frameshifted GFP/RFP in all three mutants and also restored the synergistic dependence on MBF1 and ASC1.
source: Furthermore, altering the two nucleotides downstream of the first codon pair in the three codon pair reporter reduced frameshifted GFP/RFP in all three mutants and also restored the synergistic dependence on MBF1 and ASC1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: None of three upstream changes (to the single CGA-CGG reporter) substantially reduced frameshifting.
source: By contrast, none of three upstream changes (to the single CGA-CGG reporter) substantially reduced frameshifting (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The CGA-CGG-C 7-mer is required for efficient frameshifting.
source: Thus, the CGA-CGG-C 7-mer is required for efficient frameshifting.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that changes downstream of CGA-CGG eliminate frameshifting.

claim: Frameshifted GFP/RFP was detected in asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutants in all seven yeast gene sequences tested.
source: To find out if frameshifting can occur at single CGA-CGG pairs in other sequence contexts, we tested sequences from seven yeast genes in our reporters, including six codons on either side of CGA-CGG pair. Frameshifted GFP/RFP was detected in asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutants in all cases (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: The two native sequences with CGA-CGG-C resulted in frameshifted GFP/RFP in the single mutants.
source: In particular, the two native sequences with CGA-CGG-C resulted in frameshifted GFP/RFP in the single mutants (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: CGA-CGG-C is likely a frameshifting sequence.
source: Thus, CGA-CGG-C is likely a frameshifting sequence, and contexts that allow frameshifting have not been eliminated from native genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing frameshifting at native sequences containing CGA-CGG-C.

claim: Contexts that allow frameshifting have not been eliminated from native genes.
source: Thus, CGA-CGG-C is likely a frameshifting sequence, and contexts that allow frameshifting have not been eliminated from native genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of frameshifting at native yeast gene sequences.

claim: The frameshifted protein yielded the peptide VTNLRGTTWSHPQFEK, the expected peptide from a +1 frameshift beginning with the CGA codon in the P site of the ribosome.
source: We purified the frameshifted protein, as well as an in-frame control protein with the sequence expected for a −2 frameshift at CGG (Figure 5C) and subjected them to mass spectrometry. The frameshifted protein yielded the peptide VTNLRGTTWSHPQFEK, the expected peptide from a +1 frameshift beginning with the CGA codon in the P site of the ribosome.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C by mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: Frameshift occurs with CGA in the P site, yielding only one Arg amino acid on the nascent peptide, then switches to a glycine codon GGC.
source: Thus, we infer that frameshift occurs with CGA in the P site, yielding only one Arg amino acid on the nascent peptide, then switches to a glycine codon GGC.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data identifying the frameshifted peptide sequence.

claim: Introduction of additional copies of the gene encoding tRNAArg(CCG), which decoded the in-frame CGG codon, severely reduced frameshifting.
source: To determine if aminoacyl tRNA amounts affect frameshifting, we compared the effects of additional copies of specific Arg and Gly tRNAs on frameshifting in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutant. We found that introduction of additional copies of the gene encoding tRNAArg(CCG), which decoded the in-frame CGG codon, severely reduced frameshifting (Figure 5D), as expected if arg-tRNAArg(CCG) competes with gly-tRNAGly(GCC) for the A site.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Addition of extra copies of tRNAGly(GCC) which decodes +1 frame GGC codon significantly increased frameshifting.
source: Similarly, we found that addition of extra copies of tRNAGly(GCC) which decodes +1 frame GGC codon significantly increased frameshifting in our original CGA-CGG-CAC context, as might be expect if the GGC codon is used (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Additional copies of tRNAArg(ICG), tRNAAsp(GUC), tRNAHis(GUG), tRNASer(AGA) had little or no effect on frameshifting.
source: Additional copies of tRNAArg(ICG), tRNAAsp(GUC), tRNAHis(GUG), tRNASer(AGA) had little or no effect, as expected since none of the codons decoded by these tRNAs should be occupying the A site during frameshifting.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The frameshifting occurs within the single CGA-CGG-CAC sequence and is modulated by the concentration of aminoacyl tRNAs decoding the out-of-frame codon.
source: These results indicate that the frameshifting occurs within the single CGA-CGG-CAC sequence and is modulated by the concentration of aminoacyl tRNAs decoding the out-of-frame codon.
evidence: This is inferred from the tRNA overexpression experiments showing modulation of frameshifting.

claim: Reading frame maintenance of stalled ribosomes is achieved in two ways: by direct inhibition of frameshifting; and by aborted translation coupled with mRNA decay.
source: We have uncovered a eukaryotic specific system that maintains the reading frame when ribosomes stall. Reading frame maintenance of stalled ribosomes is achieved in two ways: by direct inhibition of frameshifting; and by aborted translation coupled with mRNA decay.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing distinct roles of Mbf1/Rps3 and Asc1.

claim: The system is composed of two proteins that lack bacterial homologs, the archaeal/eukaryotic Mbf1 protein and the eukaryotic ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1, as well as one universally conserved ribosomal protein Rps3.
source: The system is composed of two proteins that lack bacterial homologs, the archaeal/eukaryotic Mbf1 protein and the eukaryotic ribosomal protein Asc1/RACK1, as well as one universally conserved ribosomal protein Rps3.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that mutations in these proteins affect frameshifting.

claim: The Rps3 residues in which mutations affect reading frame maintenance are specifically conserved in eukaryotes (and differ in archaeal and bacterial Rps3), consistent with a eukaryotic-specific mechanism.
source: Moreover, the Rps3 residues in which mutations affect reading frame maintenance are specifically conserved in eukaryotes (and differ in archaeal and bacterial Rps3), consistent with a eukaryotic-specific mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by sequence conservation analysis.

claim: When ribosomes stall, two distinct sets of events occur: Asc1 triggers a set of responses that result in aborted translation, recruitment of the RQC complex and mRNA decay; while Mbf1 and Rps3 cooperate at the stalled ribosomes to prevent frameshifting.
source: We suggest that when ribosomes stall (Simms et al., 2017b), two distinct sets of events occur: Asc1 triggers a set of responses that result in aborted translation, recruitment of the RQC complex and mRNA decay (Brandman et al., 2012; Defenouillère et al., 2013; Shao et al., 2013; Simms et al., 2017b; Sitron et al., 2017; Verma et al., 2013); while Mbf1 and Rps3 cooperate at the stalled ribosomes to prevent frameshifting (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the absence of Mbf1 and Asc1, ribosomes frameshift efficiently, even at a single CGA-CGG pair in some cases, including sequences found in the native yeast genome.
source: In the absence of Mbf1 and Asc1, ribosomes frameshift efficiently, even at a single CGA-CGG pair in some cases, including sequences found in the native yeast genome.
evidence: This is supported by data showing frameshifting at native yeast sequences in double mutants.

claim: Frameshifting on the CGA-CGG codon pair occurs in the +1 direction, with the CGA codon in the P site of the ribosome and is modulated by availability of in-frame and +1 frame A site tRNAs.
source: Frameshifting on the CGA-CGG codon pair occurs in the +1 direction, with the CGA codon in the P site of the ribosome and is modulated by availability of in-frame and +1 frame A site tRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data and tRNA overexpression experiments.

claim: The coordinated activities of both the Asc1 and Mbf1/Rps3 pathways are likely important to maintain the reading frame, since the absence of either pathway results in increased frameshifting.
source: The coordinated activities of both the Asc1 and Mbf1/Rps3 pathways are likely important to maintain the reading frame, since the absence of either pathway results in increased frameshifting.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing frameshifting in both single mutants.

claim: Both pathways are likely engaged by similar stalls, since Asc1 regulates expression at every sequence at which Mbf1 acted.
source: We think both pathways are likely engaged by similar stalls, since we noted evidence that Asc1 regulates expression (either in-frame or out-of-frame) at every sequence at which Mbf1 acted.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing overlapping effects of Asc1 and Mbf1 on the same codon pairs.

claim: At sequences at which frameshifting occurs rapidly (i.e. CGA-CGG-C), Mbf1 may play the critical role; in the absence of Mbf1, ribosomes frameshift before they can be captured by the Asc1 pathway.
source: For instance, at sequences at which frameshifting occurs rapidly (i.e. CGA-CGG-C), Mbf1 may play the critical role; in the absence of Mbf1, ribosomes frameshift before they can be captured by the Asc1 pathway.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that frameshifting at CGA-CGG-C is similar in mbf1Δ and asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutants.

claim: Some fraction of ribosomes are removed from the translating pool with concomitant mRNA decay, while ribosomes that remain stalled are kept in-frame by Mbf1/Rps3.
source: Generally, some fraction of ribosomes are removed from the translating pool with concomitant mRNA decay, while ribosomes that remain stalled are kept in-frame by Mbf1/Rps3 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The Asc1-mediated events couple mRNA decay to abortive translation, thus effectively reducing the number and duration of ribosome stalls.
source: The Asc1-mediated events couple mRNA decay to abortive translation (Sitron et al., 2017), thus effectively reducing the number and duration of ribosome stalls.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study and by the data showing increased mRNA in asc1Δ mutants.

claim: Cleavage of mRNA occurs upstream of many ribosome stalls including at CGA repeats.
source: The integration of RNA decay with translation is extensive: cleavage of mRNA occurs upstream of many ribosome stalls including at CGA repeats (Chen et al., 2010; Doma and Parker, 2006; Guydosh and Green, 2014; Letzring et al., 2010; Simms et al., 2017b) and is modulated by Asc1 (Ikeuchi and Inada, 2016; Kuroha et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mRNA cleavage is modulated by Asc1.
source: The integration of RNA decay with translation is extensive: cleavage of mRNA occurs upstream of many ribosome stalls including at CGA repeats (Chen et al., 2010; Doma and Parker, 2006; Guydosh and Green, 2014; Letzring et al., 2010; Simms et al., 2017b) and is modulated by Asc1 (Ikeuchi and Inada, 2016; Kuroha et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: mRNA decay is triggered by many problems in translation, such as nonsense mediated decay (NMD), no-go and NonStop decay.
source: mRNA decay is triggered by many problems in translation, such as nonsense mediated decay (NMD), no-go and NonStop decay [See (Shoemaker and Green, 2012; Simms et al., 2017a) and by slow translation (Presnyak et al., 2015; Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reviews and studies on mRNA decay.

claim: mRNA decay is triggered by slow translation.
source: mRNA decay is triggered by many problems in translation, such as nonsense mediated decay (NMD), no-go and NonStop decay [See (Shoemaker and Green, 2012; Simms et al., 2017a) and by slow translation (Presnyak et al., 2015; Radhakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on mRNA decay.

claim: Deletion of ASC1 in a mbf1Δ mutant results in an increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein that is directly proportional to the increase in mRNA.
source: Deletion of ASC1 in a mbf1Δ mutant results in an increase in frameshifted GFP/RFP protein that is directly proportional to the increase in mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar protein/mRNA in mbf1Δ and asc1Δ mbf1Δ mutants.

claim: asc1Δ mutants exhibit a 50-fold increase in frameshifting relative to wild type cells with less than a 3-fold increase in mRNA levels.
source: However, asc1Δ mutants exhibit a 50-fold increase in frameshifting relative to wild type cells with less than a 3-fold increase in mRNA levels.
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Figure 3A.

claim: One likely explanation for frameshifting in the asc1Δ mutant is that Mbf1 becomes limiting due to an increase in the number of stalled ribosomes.
source: One likely explanation for frameshifting in the asc1Δ mutant is that Mbf1 becomes limiting due to an increase in the number of stalled ribosomes; this idea is strengthened by the observation that overproduction of Mbf1 suppressed frameshifting in the asc1Δ mutant.
evidence: This is speculated based on the data showing that MBF1 overexpression suppresses frameshifting in asc1Δ mutants.

claim: Asc1 might also play a direct role in the reading frame maintenance function.
source: Alternatively, Asc1 might also play a direct role in the reading frame maintenance function.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that asc1Δ mutants exhibit frameshifting.

claim: Asc1 interacts with the C terminal region of Rps3 and could affect the conformation of Rps3 or its interaction with Mbf1.
source: Asc1 interacts with the C terminal region of Rps3 and could affect the conformation of Rps3 or its interaction with Mbf1.
evidence: This is speculated based on known interactions between Asc1 and Rps3.

claim: Mbf1 was found in the vicinity of Asc1.
source: Mbf1 was found in the vicinity of Asc1 (Opitz et al., 2017) lending credence to the idea that Asc1 could interact with Mbf1 (although such an interaction cannot be obligatory).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on ribosome-associated proteins.

claim: Rps3 and Mbf1 inhibit frameshifting in a coordinated manner, perhaps due to their interactions with mRNA or to Mbf1's interaction with the ribosome.
source: We think Rps3 and Mbf1 inhibit frameshifting in a coordinated manner, perhaps due to their interactions with mRNA or to Mbf1's interaction with the ribosome.
evidence: This is speculated based on the epistasis data and known properties of these proteins.

claim: The role of Rps3 in this process is likely to involve interactions with either the incoming mRNA or proteins external to the ribosome.
source: The role of Rps3 in this process is likely to involve interactions with either the incoming mRNA or proteins external to the ribosome.
evidence: This is speculated based on the location of the mutated residues on the surface of the ribosome.

claim: The RPS3 mutations that affect frameshifting map to residues (S104, L113, G121, K108) on two α-helices or their connecting loop right next to the entering mRNA.
source: The RPS3 mutations that affect frameshifting map to residues (S104, L113, G121, K108) on two α-helices or their connecting loop right next to the entering mRNA.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: This section of Rps3 is involved in helicase activity and initiation selectivity.
source: Although this section of Rps3 is involved in helicase activity and initiation selectivity (Dong et al., 2017; Takyar et al., 2005), the residues mutated in frameshifting selections were not specifically those involved in these activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on Rps3 function.

claim: The residues mutated in frameshifting selections were not specifically those involved in helicase activity and initiation selectivity.
source: Although this section of Rps3 is involved in helicase activity and initiation selectivity (Dong et al., 2017; Takyar et al., 2005), the residues mutated in frameshifting selections were not specifically those involved in these activities.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the mutated residues with those known to be involved in other functions.

claim: These residues (S104, L113, G121, K108) all sit on the solvent side of the ribosome and could form an interface interacting with mRNA or mRNA-bound proteins.
source: Instead, these residues all sit on the solvent side of the ribosome and could form an interface interacting with mRNA or mRNA-bound proteins.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural location of these residues.

claim: The role of Mbf1 is likely mediated by interactions with either or both of the mRNA and the ribosome.
source: The role of Mbf1 is likely mediated by interactions with either or both of the mRNA (Beckmann et al., 2015; Klass et al., 2013) and the ribosome (Blombach et al., 2014; Opitz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Mbf1 interactions.

claim: The apparent RNA binding domain maps to the less conserved N terminal domain.
source: The apparent RNA binding domain maps to the less conserved N terminal domain (Klass et al., 2013), while ribosome binding activity of the archaeal homolog of Mbf1 maps to its C-terminal HTH domain and the linker at the N terminus of this domain, which are both conserved with eukaryotes (Blombach et al., 2014); our frameshifting mutations cluster in the conserved linker region of Mbf1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on Mbf1 RNA binding.

evidence: This is supported by citation to structural studies of bacterial ribosomes.

claim: Frameshifting occurs by a mechanism that involves the interplay between the two adjacent codons, in which I•A wobble interaction in the P site in conjunction with competition between tRNAs entering the A site results in the frameshift.
source: Frameshifting occurs by a mechanism that involves the interplay between the two adjacent codons, in which I•A wobble interaction in the P site in conjunction with competition between tRNAs entering the A site results in the frameshift, consistent with a model proposed by Baranov et al. (Baranov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by the data on frameshifting mechanism and tRNA competition, and is consistent with a previously proposed model.

claim: Ribosomes frameshift at a single CGA-CGG codon pair (in a particular context) when the CGA codon occupies the P site in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutant.
source: First, we demonstrated that, in the asc1Δ mbf1Δ double mutant, ribosomes frameshift at a single CGA-CGG codon pair (in a particular context) when the CGA codon occupies the P site.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data identifying the frameshifted peptide.

claim: CGA codon in the P site is generally important for frameshifting, because six of the seven codon pairs on which ribosomes frameshift are CGA-NNN and the three efficient pairs are CGA-CNN.
source: We infer that CGA codon in the P site is generally important for frameshifting, because six of the seven codon pairs on which ribosomes frameshift are CGA-NNN and the three efficient pairs are CGA-CNN.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing frameshifting at multiple CGA-containing codon pairs.

source: Mutations in either RPS3 or MBF1 suppressed frameshifting mutations in several native yeast genes (Hendrick et al., 2001).
